items.heading: Here Is the Part Most
items.text: Here is the part most "food technology scope" pages soften. The brochure version of this branch and the version a real incoming batch actually experiences are describing two different starting points, and that gap is the real source of a lot of graduate disappointment later.

items.heading: "Food Technology" and "Food Science"
items.text: "Food technology" and "food science" get used almost interchangeably in casual conversation, but the admission routes into them are genuinely different, and the difference matters for later eligibility, not just the entrance exam.

rows: Fresher QA/QC trainee, mid-size food plant
A genuinely modest floor, noticeably below a fresher core-branch engineering offer at the same college tier.
Fresher, large FMCG (Nestlé, ITC, Britannia, HUL), off-campus or campus hire
The strongest entry tier, but it hires a small slice of each year's graduating pool, mostly from a handful of specialist institutes.
Pay Level 6 (roughly ₹35,400-1,12,400 basic) plus allowances, gross typically ₹4.5-7 lakh/year depending on state and posting
Government-structured pay bands with slow, predictable progression; recruitment runs through state PSCs and SSC on an irregular cycle, not every year.
QA/QC Executive or Officer, mid-size FMCG
The real fork point, generalist QC work plateaus here without a food-safety-systems, audit, or specialisation layer on top.

items.heading: College Brochures and Admission Counsellors
items.text: College brochures and admission counsellors sell food technology as "engineering plus FMCG glamour", logos of Nestlé, ITC, Britannia, and Hindustan Unilever on a placement slide, framed as if every graduate walks into one of those offices.

items.heading: IT Gets Pitched Hard As
items.text: It gets pitched hard as the "safe" branch for a student who missed the cutoff for computer science or electronics: guaranteed food demand, government backing, a real degree, no risk.

items.heading: Parents Hear "Food Industry"
items.text: Parents hear "food industry" and picture a stable, respectable, recession-proof sector, which the industry genuinely is, at the macro level.
